These national figures are general budgeting references, not a quote, advertised rate, or price cap from Great Falls Heating and Air. mainEntity.name: Should I repair my furnace or replace it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with the diagnosis. A repair may make sense if it can restore safe operation and the rest of the furnace is in reasonable condition. Repeated failures, unavailable parts, or a costly major repair can make replacement worth comparing. Age is part of the decision, along with repair history, comfort problems, warranty coverage, and the full replacement cost.

mainEntity.name: Will a heat pump keep my home warm during a Montana winter?

acceptedAnswer.text: A properly selected cold-climate heat pump can provide winter heating, but the model and your home matter. Compare how much heat it delivers in cold weather with how much your house needs. Plan any backup heat around that difference. If you’re keeping a gas or propane furnace, check that the equipment and controls can work together. A low advertised operating temperature alone doesn’t tell you whether it can heat the whole house.

mainEntity.name: Can I still claim the federal $2,000 heat pump tax credit for a 2026 installation?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The federal Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit under Section 25C is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025. Older pages advertising a heat pump credit through 2032 do not reflect that change. A qualifying 2025 installation is a separate tax-filing question; use the IRS guidance and your tax professional rather than counting a federal credit toward a new 2026 project.

mainEntity.name: Does my NorthWestern account qualify for the $450 heat pump rebate?

acceptedAnswer.text: NorthWestern’s current Montana existing-home electric application lists $450 per qualifying ducted or ductless heat pump. It requires residential electric service; a NorthWestern gas account alone does not establish eligibility. The equipment must be ENERGY STAR rated or meet SEER2 of at least 15.2 and HSPF2 of at least 8.5, along with the application’s other conditions. Confirm your account and exact models before purchase; the utility makes the final eligibility decision and funding is limited.

mainEntity.name: Do I need approval before installing a heat pump to get a Sun River Electric rebate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Sun River’s published air-source program says to request its rebate agreement and return it for approval before the contractor installs the system. It lists $150 per installed ton, capped at $750 per system, for buildings served by the cooperative. Payment follows installation and the co-op’s compliance inspection. Confirm the exact equipment, current efficiency requirements, and availability with Sun River before committing; its public page uses older SEER and HSPF terminology.

mainEntity.name: Can I apply for Montana’s HOMES or HEEHR rebates now?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not yet, according to Montana DEQ’s program page checked October 30, 2026. DEQ says the programs are not currently available and need final U.S. Department of Energy implementation approval before rollout. Announced funding or an estimated rebate is not an approval for your home. Do not assume a purchase made now will qualify later; wait for official application, timing, income, and equipment rules before relying on a future rebate.

mainEntity.name: Is NorthWestern’s up-to-$3,000 incentive for the heat pump that heats my house?

acceptedAnswer.text: That offer is for a heat pump water heater, not the space-heating heat pump. NorthWestern’s separate program requires an existing electric resistance water-heater tank and a participating contractor; replacing a gas water heater does not qualify. Home type, age, account, and other restrictions apply, with one incentive per residence and limited funding. Confirm the current requirements and participating contractor before ordering; this page does not establish Great Falls Heating and Air’s enrollment in that program.

mainEntity.name: What paperwork and deadlines should I confirm before counting a rebate in my budget?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use the application for your utility account and project, and check approval timing before buying. NorthWestern’s current existing-home electric form excludes work completed or materials purchased before August 1, 2026, and requires project completion and submission by June 30, 2027, with a recent bill and itemized receipts or invoices. Other programs have different steps, so keep model details, approvals, invoices, and a copy of the submitted application. Do not subtract an unapproved incentive from the amount you must be able to pay, and ask each administrator before assuming incentives can be combined.

mainEntity.name: Why is my furnace running but blowing cold air?

acceptedAnswer.text: Check whether the thermostat fan is set to ON. That setting can circulate room-temperature air between heating cycles. If the house is losing heat, an airflow restriction, ignition problem, fuel-supply issue, or safety shutdown may need diagnosis. The symptom alone doesn’t tell you which part has failed. Keep panels closed and don’t bypass safety switches or keep resetting the furnace. Call for service if it won’t heat. If you smell gas or a CO alarm sounds, leave immediately and call 911 from a safe location. Background: Carrier: reasons a furnace blows cold air.

mainEntity.name: Why does my furnace keep shutting off, especially in windy or freezing weather?

acceptedAnswer.text: Restricted airflow, an ignition or control fault, or a venting problem can interrupt heating. Wind and snow around outside intake or exhaust openings are useful details to report, but they don’t prove the cause. Tell us when the furnace stops, whether it restarts, and whether the indoor temperature is falling. From ground level, look for loose snow blocking accessible vents. Clear only loose snow you can safely reach. Don’t climb, chip ice, disconnect venting, or bypass a safety switch. If it keeps shutting down, stop troubleshooting and call. For gas odor or a CO alarm, leave immediately and call 911 from outside. Background: Trane: furnace shutdown and lockout.

mainEntity.name: Should I repair an older furnace or replace it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with what’s wrong and whether a repair can restore safe operation. Compare the repair price with the furnace’s condition, repair history, available parts, and any warranty coverage. Repeated failures or a major repair may make replacement worth considering, but age alone doesn’t settle the decision. If some rooms stay cold, the ductwork, insulation, or airflow may also need attention. A new furnace alone may not solve that problem. Compare the full installation work in our furnace replacement guide. Background: ENERGY STAR: when to consider replacement or system improvements.

mainEntity.name: Does my furnace need an inspection every year if it still works?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. CPSC recommends a professional inspection of fuel-burning heating systems each year, including furnaces. Follow your equipment’s maintenance instructions too. A furnace producing heat can still have a problem that needs attention. Ask what the visit includes and whether cleaning, filters, or repairs are priced separately. Maintenance can identify concerns, but it can’t guarantee a winter without breakdowns. See our furnace maintenance guide for the checks to discuss. Source: CPSC: annual heating-system inspections.

mainEntity.name: What can I safely check before calling for furnace repair?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you smell gas, hear a CO alarm, or suspect a gas or carbon monoxide leak, leave immediately and call 911 or your gas utility from outside. Otherwise, keep checks to the homeowner tasks your equipment instructions allow: Thermostat: Check that HEAT is selected, the setting is above room temperature, and a schedule isn’t explaining the change. Filter: Check an accessible filter. Turn the system off as instructed before changing it, use the correct size and type, and don’t run without a filter. Power: Note whether the external furnace switch is off or a breaker has tripped. Don’t open electrical compartments or repeatedly reset a tripping breaker. Visible code: Note a fault code only if it is visible without removing panels. Share it when you call; don’t bypass a door switch to read it. If the furnace still won’t heat, call for 24/7 emergency service and repair. Don’t wait for a form reply when your home is losing heat. Background: Carrier: thermostat, airflow, and professional service checks.

mainEntity.name: Can I keep my gas furnace and add a heat pump for Montana winters?

acceptedAnswer.text: Possibly. A dual-fuel system uses a heat pump with a compatible gas or propane furnace. The furnace’s condition, indoor coil, blower, ductwork, electrical supply, and controls all need to work with the proposed equipment. Compare the heat pump’s output in cold weather with your home’s heating needs, then plan how the furnace will take over when needed. The settings depend on the equipment and your fuel costs; there isn’t one changeover temperature for every Great Falls home. Our cold-climate heat pump guide explains the options. mainEntity.name: My furnace works after a reset, then stops again. Should I keep resetting it?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A reset may restart the furnace without resolving the fault that shut it down. If it locks out again, stop troubleshooting and call. Follow only the homeowner instructions for your exact model; don’t bypass safety switches, reset rollout switches, or remove panels. Note any code visible through a sight glass before interrupting power. If you smell gas, see smoke, or hear a CO alarm, leave immediately and call 911 from a safe location.

mainEntity.name: What do the blinking red or amber lights on my furnace mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: The meaning depends on the furnace’s brand, model, and blink pattern. There isn’t one universal three-flash or four-flash diagnosis. If the light is visible through a sight glass without opening the cabinet, note or photograph the pattern and share it with the model number when you call. Keep panels in place and don’t hold down a door switch to read a code. A code helps guide testing; it doesn’t prove which part needs replacing.

mainEntity.name: Can I use a space heater while waiting for furnace repair?

acceptedAnswer.text: A portable electric heater can provide temporary warmth if you follow its instructions. Put it on a stable, level, nonflammable surface and keep it at least three feet from bedding, curtains, furniture, and other things that can burn. Keep children and pets away. Plug it directly into a suitable wall outlet, never an extension cord or power strip. Stop using it if the plug or outlet gets hot or a breaker trips. Turn it off before sleeping or leaving the room. Never use an oven, grill, outdoor heater, or generator indoors for heat.

mainEntity.name: How do I keep my pipes from freezing while the furnace is out?

acceptedAnswer.text: Open kitchen and bathroom sink-cabinet doors so any remaining warmer room air can reach the plumbing. Move cleaning products out of children’s and pets’ reach, and keep garage doors closed if water lines run through the garage. These steps can reduce exposure but won’t guarantee pipes stay unfrozen as the house cools. Follow your water utility’s guidance and call a plumber for suspected frozen or burst pipes. Never use an open flame to thaw a pipe. If you need to leave the house, ask about protecting the plumbing before you go; don’t leave a portable heater running unattended.

mainEntity.name: What size furnace do I need? Should I get the same BTUs as the old one?

acceptedAnswer.text: The old rating is useful information, but it isn’t a sizing calculation. New windows, added insulation, air leaks, or a finished room can change how much heat your house needs. Ask for a load calculation using the home’s current condition and local winter design conditions. Compare the selected furnace’s heating output, not just its fuel-input rating, and follow its altitude requirements. A bigger furnace won’t automatically fix a cold bedroom; airflow and insulation may need attention too.

mainEntity.name: Is a two-stage furnace worth the extra cost? Is that the same as variable speed?

acceptedAnswer.text: They describe different features. A two-stage burner has lower and higher heating outputs; a variable-speed blower adjusts airflow. The right combination may improve comfort in a suitable system, but it won’t automatically fix duct problems or guarantee lower bills. Ask what difference the upgrade should make in your home. Compare the added price, controls, noise, service needs, and warranty terms before paying for features you may not need.

mainEntity.name: Should I choose an 80% furnace or a high-efficiency condensing furnace?

acceptedAnswer.text: Compare the installation work along with the AFUE efficiency rating. A non-condensing furnace needs suitable combustion air and venting. A condensing furnace also needs approved venting and a way to handle condensate, with freeze protection where needed. A finished basement, exterior vent route, or shared water-heater chimney can change the work involved. Compare the full installed price, expected fuel use, and the equipment that fits your home. The efficiency percentage alone won’t tell you what your bills will be.

mainEntity.name: Can I replace just the furnace and keep my existing air conditioner?

acceptedAnswer.text: Possibly. The new furnace’s blower, indoor cooling coil, controls, and duct airflow need to work with your existing AC. Have the equipment checked together before deciding what stays. Ask which parts can be reused, which need changing, and how both heating and cooling will be tested. If you expect to replace the AC later or add a heat pump, mention that now so the furnace proposal accounts for that plan. Replacing one system doesn’t automatically mean replacing both.

mainEntity.name: Will my gas water heater need changes if the new furnace stops using the chimney?

acceptedAnswer.text: It needs a venting assessment, even if you’re keeping the water heater. Removing the furnace changes the appliances using the chimney. The remaining vent may need changes so the water heater can vent safely; it isn’t automatically safe to leave it as it was. Ask what was checked and have any required venting work and safety tests included in the written proposal. A furnace replacement doesn’t automatically require a new water heater, but it does require looking at how the remaining appliance will vent.

mainEntity.name: How long will furnace replacement take, and will I be without heat overnight?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask for the schedule for your actual job before the old furnace is disconnected. Equipment access, duct changes, venting, electrical work, inspections, and parts can affect completion. For a winter replacement, agree on safe temporary arrangements and what happens if the work runs longer. Don’t assume same-day completion, loan heaters, or overnight heat unless those arrangements are confirmed. Before the job is complete, ask for startup results, operating instructions, filter details, and warranty and registration responsibilities.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a permit for furnace replacement, and who handles it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Confirm the requirements for your installation address before work starts. Great Falls publishes mechanical-permit forms, while projects outside a certified local jurisdiction follow the state’s rules, including applicable residential exemptions. Don’t assume the city process applies to every rural home. Ask the relevant building department what is required, and have the proposal state who handles any permits, fees, inspections, and corrections. A homeowner application isn’t automatically the right form for a contractor’s installation.

mainEntity.name: Why is my upstairs hot when the basement and main floor are cool?

acceptedAnswer.text: The system may be cooling while air isn’t reaching the rooms that need it. Sun exposure, insulation, duct leaks, return-air paths, thermostat location, and airflow can all matter. Tell us which rooms overheat, when it happens, and whether doors are usually closed. Keep grilles clear, but don’t close a group of downstairs vents or change blower settings to force air upstairs. Have the airflow and room conditions assessed before assuming a bigger AC or a new part will fix the problem.

mainEntity.name: Can I run my AC during wildfire smoke, and will it filter the smoke out?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cooling can help you keep windows closed during a smoke event, but fine-smoke removal needs suitable filtration. For central systems, EPA recommends MERV 13 or the highest efficiency the system can accommodate. Check compatibility, fit, and filter condition; a higher rating alone doesn’t mean a filter suits your blower. Inspect more often during heavy smoke. A properly sized portable air cleaner can help. Standard ductless washable screens aren’t a substitute for fine-particle filtration. Follow current local guidance, and seek a cooler location if you can’t keep the home comfortably cool.

mainEntity.name: Can I wash cottonwood fluff off my outdoor AC unit myself?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only do the cleaning your exact model’s owner instructions permit. Turn the system off and follow its power-isolation instructions first; turning down the thermostat doesn’t isolate electrical power. Keep loose debris away and use only the coil’s approved gentle cleaning method. Don’t remove the fan or panels, spray electrical components, use a pressure washer, or force a brush into the fins. Matted fluff, difficult access, or an unfamiliar unit are reasons to arrange professional cleaning. A clean-looking cabinet alone doesn’t tell you the coil is clear.

mainEntity.name: Should I repair my older air conditioner or replace it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with the diagnosis, equipment condition, repair history, parts availability, warranty, and written repair price. A repair may make sense for an otherwise sound system. Repeated failures or a major repair can make replacement worth comparing. Age alone doesn’t settle it. If the main problem is one hot room, assess airflow and the house too. When replacement makes sense, compare the full installation work for standard AC and a heat pump, including existing-furnace compatibility and expected heating use. Confirm any rebate separately before counting it toward the price.

mainEntity.name: Do refrigerant rules mean I have to replace my working R-410A air conditioner?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. EPA says existing systems can continue to be used and repaired as refrigerants are phased down. That doesn’t guarantee every part or refrigerant will always be available at the same price. Have the actual refrigerant and compatible repair options identified before deciding. A different refrigerant isn’t automatically suitable for your equipment, and recharging isn’t routine upkeep for a leaking system. Ask what caused any refrigerant loss, what repair is proposed, and how operation will be checked afterward.

mainEntity.name: Why is my AC running but blowing warm air?

acceptedAnswer.text: The fan can move air even when the system isn’t cooling properly. Thermostat settings, restricted airflow, outdoor-unit trouble, icing, or refrigerant performance may be involved. Note whether all rooms are warm, whether the outdoor unit runs, and any visible ice or alerts without opening equipment. Those observations help guide testing; they don’t prove which part failed. Check only the controls and accessible filter your owner instructions allow. If you see ice, stop cooling. For smoke, sparking, or a burning smell, stay clear; leave and call 911 for fire or immediate danger.

mainEntity.name: My outdoor AC unit is humming but the fan won’t spin. Is it the capacitor?

acceptedAnswer.text: A capacitor is one possibility, but a motor, power-supply, control, or another fault can produce similar symptoms. Switch cooling off through the normal controls and arrange service. Don’t push the blades with a stick, reach through the grille, remove covers, or try to replace a capacitor yourself. Electrical components can remain hazardous after power is switched off. Ask what the electrical and operating tests found before approving a part replacement; the sound alone isn’t a diagnosis.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if the AC lines or indoor coil are frozen?

acceptedAnswer.text: Switch cooling off and call for guidance. Use fan-only mode only if the blower operates normally and your equipment instructions allow it. Don’t chip ice, apply heat, remove panels, or keep restarting cooling. Stay clear of water near electrical equipment and report where it appears. The system may need to thaw before useful testing can be completed, but thawing doesn’t fix the cause. Airflow, blower operation, refrigerant performance, or another fault may need assessment. There is no guaranteed thawing time or first-visit repair.

mainEntity.name: If my AC is low on refrigerant, can you just top it off?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask how the low charge was established and why it is low. A leak or an incorrect earlier charge may need investigation. Discuss the testing, repair access, compatible refrigerant, and how operation will be checked afterward. Leak detection, parts, and refrigerant may involve separate work and pricing. Review those costs before approval. Leave refrigerant connections and charging to a qualified technician.

Confirm any incentive separately with your utility before relying on it, and agree on the price of extra work before approving it.

mainEntity.name: Will installation leave visible pipes or require a drain pump?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask the installer to show the indoor-unit positions, line routes, wall or ceiling openings, and drain destination before work begins. Some locations allow gravity drainage, while others need a suitable condensate pump with access for maintenance. Confirm which piping and covers will be visible, how penetrations will be sealed, and who handles patching or finish repairs. A clean-looking indoor unit still needs filter and service access; do not assume every route can be hidden inside a wall.

mainEntity.name: Is cleaning the washable filters enough to maintain a mini-split?

acceptedAnswer.text: Filter care is only part of maintenance. Follow the exact model’s owner instructions for permitted cleaning, safe shutdown, filter type, and frequency; keep that access clear of furniture. Coils, blower components, drains, any fitted pump, and outdoor equipment also need appropriate inspection and service. Ask what a maintenance visit includes and whether deeper cleaning costs extra, and leave electrical work, refrigerant handling, and unfamiliar disassembly to a qualified technician.

mainEntity.name: Is ice or steam on my outdoor heat pump normal, or does it need repair?

acceptedAnswer.text: Light frost and a temporary vapor cloud can accompany normal defrost, with changes in fan operation or sound. Persistent ice, a fan striking ice, falling indoor temperature, or repeated alerts deserve a service call rather than an assumption that the unit will clear itself. Do not chip ice, apply heat, force a defrost cycle, or open the cabinet. If you suspect smoke, burning, or sparking, stay clear and stop troubleshooting; for fire or immediate danger, leave and call 911 from a safe place.

mainEntity.name: Why is AUX heat coming on more often, and should I turn it off?

acceptedAnswer.text: Auxiliary or backup heat can operate because of outdoor conditions, heating demand, thermostat recovery, defrost, the configured control strategy, or a fault. An AUX message alone does not identify the cause, and there is no universal temperature at which it proves something is wrong. Note when it appears, recent schedule or setpoint changes, whether the house stays warm, and any change in total energy use. Do not disable backup heat or change installer settings to hide the message; ask for the system’s intended operation to be compared with actual findings.

mainEntity.name: My heat pump is running but blowing cool air. What can I check safely?

acceptedAnswer.text: If there are no danger signs, note the thermostat mode, setpoint, schedule, alerts, indoor temperature, and whether all rooms or only one zone are affected. Brief cooler air can occur during defrost, but persistent loss of heat needs assessment. Check accessible filters and grilles only as your owner instructions allow, and observe outdoor snow or debris from outside the cabinet. Do not open panels, touch wiring or refrigerant connections, or repeatedly reset a breaker; call promptly if the home is losing heat or you are unsure what to do.

mainEntity.name: How often should a heat pump be serviced, and what should maintenance include?

acceptedAnswer.text: Follow the exact model’s maintenance schedule and discuss service before the heating and cooling seasons when the equipment is used year-round. Confirm checks for the relevant filters, coils, airflow, drainage, electrical components, operating performance, controls, and backup coordination. Ask for a record of completed work, findings, available readings, and any tests limited by weather or equipment condition. Ductless deep cleaning, difficult access, further diagnosis, and repairs may be separate work; maintenance cannot guarantee no later breakdowns or warranty coverage.

mainEntity.name: How much will heat pump diagnosis or repair cost, and is it included in a tune-up?

acceptedAnswer.text: Confirm the diagnostic fee and what it covers before booking; do not assume a tune-up includes fault diagnosis, deep cleaning, leak testing, or repairs. The actual price depends on the fault, parts, labor, access, applicable warranty, and any additional testing or visits. General online prices are budgeting references, not a quote, advertised rate, or price cap from Great Falls Heating and Air; actual costs may be lower or substantially higher. Ask for the findings, proposed repair, exclusions, and price before approval, including whether any diagnostic charge is credited toward repair.

mainEntity.name: Should I repair my heat pump or replace it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with the diagnosis, written repair price, equipment condition, repair history, compatible parts availability, and any applicable warranty. Ask whether airflow, controls, installation, or room-coverage problems also need attention and how the repair will be checked. Compare that with a complete replacement quote when the findings warrant it, rather than deciding from an age cutoff, alert code, or rebate alone. Confirm parts timing and any follow-up, and keep projected operating savings separate from measured results.
